### **Introduction**

In your previous lessons, you learned about inheritance and method overriding. A child class can get attributes and methods from a parent class, and can override a method it inherits to give the method its own behavior. Let's connect these ideas to another principle in Object-oriented programming, polymorphism. 

Polymorphism in Python allows the same method, function, or operator to behave differently depending on the object it operates on. It makes the code more flexible and reusable. One way to achieve polymorphism is through inheritance and method overriding, where a child class provides its own version of a method already defined in the parent class. Python chooses the right version based on the object's type.

In this study guide, you will learn the different types of polymorphism and how it helps make programs more flexible, organized, and easier to improve.

### **Module Learning Objectives **

After working on this module, you should be able to:

1. Define polymorphism in object-oriented programming.  
2. Explain how polymorphism relates to inheritance and method overriding.  
3. Create a simple program applying polymorphism in a real-life scenario.

### **Key Concepts and Learning Activities**

** **  
Polymorphism is a fancy Greek word that literally means "many forms" (poly \= many, morph \= form). It is one of the principles in Object-oriented programming.

Polymorphism allows the same name to do different things depending on what you give it. Think of it like the word "Play": you "play" a song in a music app, play a movie in a video app, and start a game on a game console. The command is the same, play, but the result changes based on what you are using.  

Here are the three main ways you'll see polymorphism in action:

***1.1 Polymorphism with Built-in Functions*** 

Python uses polymorphism even without classes. Python has built-in functions that handle objects based on their data types. Examples are the len() and max() built-in functions.  

**len()** function:  This function is used to determine the number of items (the length or size) within an object. 

Strings:   **len("Hi"**) counts characters (2).  
Lists:       **len(\[1, 2, 3\])** counts items (3).

Python code:   
![][image1]  
On a string, len() counts the total number of characters, including spaces and punctuation; on a list, len() counts the number of individual items.


     **max()** function: This function finds the largest item in a list. The "logic" of what is "larger" changes based on the data type.

		Numbers: **max(10, 30, 50\)**   returns 50  (highest mathematical value)

                        Strings:    **max(“Pineapple”, “Banana”)**  returns “Pineapple”  

                                        (based alphabetical order)

Python code:

![][image2]

    **\+ operator:** The **\+** sign is also a classic example of "one tool, many uses". If you give it two numbers, it performs addition. If you give it two strings, it performs concatenation (joining them). 	

Numbers: 5 \+ 5 gives you 10 (math).

Strings: "Hot" \+ "Dog" gives you "HotDog" (joining).

This page on the Great Learning website discusses the ways polymorphism is used in Python. Read the part that explains Polymorphism in built-in functions (3 minutes).

***1.2 Polymorphism with Inheritance (Method Overriding)*** 

By now, you should already understand what method overriding is and how to use it to change how a method works in a child class. Method overriding occurs when a child class uses the same method name as in the parent class but gives it a different implementation. 

Method overriding is an example of polymorphism, which means “many forms.” Even though the method name is the same, it can perform different actions depending on which class is using it. 

In the Zoo Management System from the previous module, the **make\_sound()** and **eat()** methods of the parent class Animal were overridden in the child classes Lion, Elephant, and Monkey to implement each animal's specific behaviors. In the Hospital Billing System, **calculate\_bill()** was modified to apply an appropriate discount based on the patient type: Senior Citizen and Philhealth Member. 

The same method name behaved differently across objects. This makes programs more flexible, organized, and easier to improve.

Method overriding is classified as a form of run-time polymorphism. Find out more about this in the learning resource below. 

	**Learning resource 2:** [Polymorphism in Python](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/polymorphism-in-python/)  
This page on the GeeksforGeeks website presents method overriding as a run-time form of polymorphism. Read the sub-section with the title “Runtime Polymorphism (Overriding)” (3 minutes).

***1.3 Polymorphism with Class Methods (Duck Typing)***

In Python, polymorphism doesn't always need inheritance. You can create different classes with the same method name that perform different behaviors. Python can call these methods even if they are not part of a class hierarchy. 

The idea is called **Duck-Typing**.  Its philosophy is "**If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck**.” This means that if the object has the needed method, Python can use it regardless of what class it comes from.  It makes your code more flexible because you don't have to change your classes to fit a certain structure.  Learn about Duck Typing in the following video.

### **Key takeaways**

Polymorphism lets one method or function do different things depending on the object. Same name, different behavior.  

When a child class overrides a method inherited from a parent, is an example of polymorphism. Method overriding is a type of polymorphism.

Polymorphism works even without inheritance.  Even unrelated classes can have methods with the same name, and Python will call the correct version based on the object. 

Storing different objects in a list and calling the same method on each object clearly demonstrates polymorphism. Python automatically runs the version of the method that belongs to that specific object.

Polymorphism simplifies code. It makes programs easier to read and maintain because the same code can handle different object types.
